rows.question: We need a security agent on every GPU worker but nowhere else. Which controller and scheduling constraint should we use?
rows.answer: To ensure a security agent runs on every GPU worker node and nowhere else, you should use a DaemonSet controller. You can achieve this by setting a node affinity constraint in the DaemonSet's Pod specification to match only the GPU worker nodes. This can be done by specifying the node affinity in the .spec.template.spec.affinity.nodeAffinity field to target nodes with a specific label that identifies them as GPU workers.
contexts:
[Evidence source: concepts__workloads__controllers__daemonset.html]
How Daemon Pods are scheduledA DaemonSet can be used to ensure that all eligible nodes run a copy of a Pod. The DaemonSet controller creates a Pod for each eligible node and adds the spec.affinity.nodeAffinity field of the Pod to match the target host. After the Pod is created, the default scheduler typically takes over and then binds the Pod to the target host by setting the .spec.nodeName field. If the new Pod cannot fit on the node, the default scheduler may preempt (evict) some of the existing Pods based on the priority of the new Pod.Note:If it's important that the DaemonSet pod run on each node, it's often desirable to set the .spec.template.spec.priorityClassName of the DaemonSet to a PriorityClass with a higher priority to ensure that this eviction occurs.The user can specify a different scheduler for the Pods of the DaemonSet, by setting the .spec.template.spec.schedulerName field of the DaemonSet.

rows.ground_truth: Use a DaemonSet so Kubernetes maintains one agent Pod on each eligible node. Add a node selector, node affinity, or equivalent node-label constraint matching GPU workers so other nodes are not eligible for the DaemonSet Pods.

rows.question: Only frontend Pods may call the payments Pods on TCP 8443, and payments must not initiate other egress. What policy model expresses this?
rows.answer: The context does not provide exact YAML configurations for the specific scenario described. However, based on the provided context, you can create a NetworkPolicy to allow only frontend Pods to access payments Pods on TCP 8443 by specifying an ingress rule for the payments Pods that allows traffic from Pods with the frontend label on port 8443. Additionally, to prevent payments Pods from initiating any egress traffic, you can create a default deny egress policy for the payments Pods. The exact YAML syntax for these policies is not provided in the context.
contexts:
[Evidence source: concepts__services-networking__network-policies.html]
Allow all ingress trafficIf you want to allow all incoming connections to all pods in a namespace, you can create a policy that explicitly allows that.service/networking/network-policy-allow-all-ingress.yaml --- apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: NetworkPolicy metadata: name: allow-all-ingress spec: podSelector: {} ingress: - {} policyTypes: - Ingress With this policy in place, no additional policy or policies can cause any incoming connection to those pods to be denied. This policy has no effect on isolation for egress from any pod.Default deny all egress trafficYou can create a "default" egress isolation policy for a namespace by creating a NetworkPolicy that selects all pods but does not allow any egress traffic from those pods.service/networking/network-policy-default-deny-egress.yaml --- apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: NetworkPolicy metadata: name: default-deny-egress spec: podSelector: {} policyTypes: - Egress This ensures that even pods that aren't selected by any

[Evidence source: concepts__services-networking__network-policies.html]
When a pod is isolated for ingress, the only allowed connections into the pod are those from the pod's node and those allowed by the ingress list of some NetworkPolicy that applies to the pod for ingress. Reply traffic for those allowed connections will also be implicitly allowed. The effects of those ingress lists combine additively.Network policies do not conflict; they are additive. If any policy or policies apply to a given pod for a given direction, the connections allowed in that direction from that pod is the union of what the applicable policies allow. Thus, order of evaluation does not affect the policy result.For a connection from a source pod to a destination pod to be allowed, both the egress policy on the source pod and the ingress policy on the destination pod need to allow the connection. If either side does not allow the connection, it will not happen.The NetworkPolicy resourceSee the NetworkPolicy reference for a full definition of the resource.

[Evidence source: concepts__services-networking__network-policies.html]
Concepts › Services-Networking › Network-Policies Concepts › Services-Networking › Network-Policies Network Policies | Kubernetes Network PoliciesIf you want to control traffic flow at the IP address or port level (OSI layer 3 or 4), NetworkPolicies allow you to specify rules for traffic flow within your cluster, and also between Pods and the outside world. Your cluster must use a network plugin that supports NetworkPolicy enforcement.If you want to control traffic flow at the IP address or port level for TCP, UDP, and SCTP protocols, then you might consider using Kubernetes NetworkPolicies for particular applications in your cluster. NetworkPolicies are an application-centric construct which allow you to specify how a pod is allowed to communicate with various network "entities" (we use the word "entity" here to avoid overloading the more common terms such as "endpoints" and "services", which have specific Kubernetes connotations) over the network.
rows.ground_truth: Apply NetworkPolicies enforced by a compatible network plugin. Select the payments Pods, allow ingress on TCP 8443 only from frontend Pods selected by labels, and apply an egress-isolating policy with only explicitly required exceptions. Policies are additive, so account for every policy selecting the Pods.
